extra_misconceptions.fact: Current pins feet-first swimmers under branches; swim aggressively head-first toward a strainer to climb up and over the trunk.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimming feet-first into a downed tree strainer protects your head and lets you push off the branches safely.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Low-head dams create uniform, bank-to-bank recirculating hydraulics with no escape channels, making them deadly drowning machines.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Low-head dams are safer than natural waterfalls because their smooth concrete drop is only a few feet high.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leaning upstream drops the upstream gunwale, allowing current to catch the hull, swamp the boat, and wrap it around the rock.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaning away from an obstacle rock keeps your face clear of impact when a canoe or kayak pins sideways.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water conducts heat away from the body 25 times faster than air, so cold water causes rapid hypothermia even on warm, sunny days.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hypothermia is only a concern on whitewater trips when the air temperature drops below fifty degrees Fahrenheit.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a swimmer who tries to stand up in knee-deep current moving faster than a brisk walk?
Which physical indicator warns you that a low-head dam has a recirculating boil line below its drop?
Why is it dangerous to lean upstream when your boat pins sideways against a midstream boulder or strainer?
What combined water and air temperature threshold requires thermal protection to prevent cold-water shock?

extra_misconceptions.fact: An upstream V forms where water parts around an obstacle right at the apex, whereas a downstream V points into the open channel.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An upstream V pointing toward the source of the river marks the deepest, cleanest channel between two rocks.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Friction against the streambed and banks slows the water, so the fastest current flows near the surface in the deepest main channel.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: River water flows at the exact same speed from the surface down to the rocky streambed and from bank to bank.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water in a strong eddy circulates upstream toward the obstacle, creating a shear zone along the eddy line where currents meet.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Water inside an eddy behind a boulder is completely stagnant and does not move in any direction.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standing waves remain over fixed riverbed contours as fast shallow water decelerates into deeper, slower water below a chute.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standing waves in a rapid travel downstream with the current just like ocean waves rolling toward a beach.

extra_socratic_questions: What surface flow pattern distinguishes a passable downstream V chute from a hazardous upstream V rock?
Where on a river bend does the fastest current travel, and where do gravel bars and eddies typically form?
Under what riverbed condition does a series of stationary standing waves form downstream of a constriction?
Why does a sharp horizon line across the entire river channel require scouting from shore before proceeding?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Moving water requires instant lateral boat placement, edge control, and bracing strokes that must be automatic on flatwater first.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Strong flatwater forward paddling is enough to steer through rapids without practicing lateral draws or braces.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You must lean forward, locate and pull the spray skirt grab loop forward and up first, and then push out of the cockpit heels-first.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: In a kayak wet exit, you should push your body out of the cockpit before pulling the spray skirt grab loop.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Kneeling on the hull bottom with thighs wedged against the gunwales drops your center of gravity and locks your body to the canoe.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sitting high on a canoe bench seat lowers your center of gravity and gives better balance in turbulent water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stern rudders bleed momentum and only pivot the boat; draw and pry strokes are required to shift the hull laterally across current.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Flatwater rudder strokes at the stern are the fastest way to move a boat sideways away from a sudden river obstacle.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to hull stability on moving water if a paddler powers strokes only with their arms instead of torso rotation?
Which blade angle adjustment during a J-stroke or stern sweep keeps a solo or tandem craft tracking straight on flatwater?
Why is it dangerous to enter even Class I moving water before demonstrating a calm-water wet exit and boat recovery?
What body posture and knee contact inside your boat confirm you are ready to transition from flatwater to current?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Lifting your head first collapses the brace; you must snap your hips and knees to roll the hull flat before bringing your head up last.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling your head up first to look at the sky is the key motion that brings a tipping boat upright during a brace.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Torso rotation into a cross bow draw keeps both hands locked in position and applies immediate blade power without losing a beat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Switching paddle hands across the gunwale is faster and more stable than rotating your torso into a cross bow draw.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A low brace uses the back face of the blade flat on the water with knuckles rolled down and elbows bent above the paddle shaft.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A low brace relies on pushing down with the power face of the paddle blade while holding your wrists straight.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Over-prying the stern swings the tail wide into obstacles; bow and stern paddlers must coordinate draws and pries to pivot cleanly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: In a tandem canoe, the stern paddler should initiate bow turns by prying the stern violently in the opposite direction.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your shoulder joint during a high brace if your elbows rise above shoulder height in strong current?
Why does a cross bow draw move the bow toward your offside without requiring you to switch hands on the paddle grip?
Which face of the paddle blade contacts the water during a low brace, and how does your hip snap right the boat?
Under what clearance condition should a canoeist choose a sculling draw instead of a deep, wide bow pry near rocks?

extra_misconceptions.fact: High water can wash out eddies and turn Class II waves into Class IV hydraulics, while low water exposes jagged rocks and pinning hazards.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A river section's International Scale rating is permanent and stays the same regardless of rainfall or dam releases.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Clear, wide channels without scouting define Class II; Class III features irregular waves, tight passages, and complex eddy turns.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Class III whitewater means the rapids have clear, obvious channels that require no maneuvering or scouting.

extra_misconceptions.fact: River ratings combine gradient, flow volume, constriction width, obstacle complexity, water temperature, and remoteness from rescue.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The International Scale of River Difficulty measures only the steepness of the riverbed gradient in feet per mile.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Moderate rises can actually pad out shallow rock gardens, though extreme flows create powerful keepers and eliminate recovery eddies.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Higher water volume always makes a rapid more difficult by increasing the height of every rock obstacle in the bed.

extra_socratic_questions: What channel characteristics and rescue conditions separate a Class II novice rapid from a Class III intermediate rapid?
What happens to the International Scale rating of a rocky Class II rapid when heavy rain triples the cubic feet per second?
Which gauge measurement confirms whether a river stretch is running at low bony levels or high flood stage before launch?
Under what environmental or cold-water conditions can a technical Class II rapid present Class III consequences for swimmers?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Universal river signals always use positive direction: point your paddle at a 45-degree angle toward the open side to run.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pointing your paddle toward a midstream boulder tells following boaters which obstacle they need to avoid.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Moving arms horizontally side to side or holding a paddle horizontally signals Stop; a vertical paddle blade signals All clear.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Waving your arms side to side above your head is the standard signal telling the next boat to come ahead.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rushing whitewater drowns out human voices within a few boat lengths, making sharp whistle blasts and high-contrast hand signals vital.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Shouting voice commands down a rapid is reliable enough that paddlers do not need whistles or paddle signals.

extra_misconceptions.fact: River left and river right are always referenced facing downstream in the direction of the current flow, never facing upstream.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: River left and river right are determined by looking upstream from the bottom of a rapid toward oncoming boats.

extra_socratic_questions: Why must a scout point toward the safe eddy or channel rather than pointing at the hazard when signaling a line?
What happens to communication if a swimmer simply looks at a rescuer without patting the top of their helmet?
Which paddle blade orientation tells upstream boats to stop and wait versus signaling that the channel is all clear?
What whistle blast pattern signals an emergency requiring immediate help over the roar of a turbulent rapid?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A protruding keel catches on cross-currents and trips the hull on sideways eddies; whitewater hulls use smooth bottoms and high rocker.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A long, straight-keeled lake canoe is ideal for technical whitewater because the keel holds a straight line in waves.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Flotation bags displace hundreds of pounds of water so a swamped boat rides high, resists rock wraps, and can be rescued quickly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Flotation bags are installed in whitewater canoes and kayaks solely to keep the empty boat from sinking to the bottom.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Creek boats use high bow volume and rounded decks to resurface cleanly after steep drops and shed water that would pin a playboat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Low-volume slicey playboats are safer than high-volume creek boats in steep, rocky drops because they weigh less.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Deep hulls with flared sides and upturned ends deflect splashing waves outward and climb over haystacks instead of plowing through.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A canoe with low, flat sides and low ends stays drier in big standing waves than a deeper hull with flared sides.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a canoe's turning agility and straight-line tracking when hull rocker increases from flat to four inches?
Why do whitewater kayaks and solo river canoes use rotomolded polyethylene or ABS composites instead of brittle fiberglass?
Which hull cross-section profile provides sharper eddy-line carving, a rounded bottom or a flat planing hull with chines?
Where should flotation air bags be secured in an open whitewater canoe to prevent the hull from wrapping on a rock?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Never tie a fixed rope to your body in current; hold the rope or use a quick-release harness so you are not dragged underwater.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying a rescue throw rope directly around your waist ensures you will not drop the line when catching a swimmer.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cotton absorbs water and strips body heat rapidly when wet; paddlers must layer synthetic fleece, wool, wetsuits, or drysuits.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cotton sweatshirts and denim jeans provide warm backup insulation under a rain jacket on chilly whitewater trips.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Sturdy closed-toe river shoes protect feet from sharp rocks and glass and provide critical traction when scouting or wading rescues.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Flip-flops or bare feet are safer than closed-toe river shoes because they slip off easily if a foot catches.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coiled loops twist and knot mid-throw; always stuff the rope into the bag inch by inch so it feeds out without tangling.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Coiling a throw rope neatly into loops before placing it into the bag helps the line pay out smoothly during a toss.

extra_socratic_questions: What test confirms your Type III or Type V PFD is buckled tightly enough to keep your chin above aerated whitewater?
Why is it dangerous to wear a recreational cycling helmet instead of a water-specific helmet rated for river impacts?
Where should a paddler carry a rescue throw bag on deck so it deploys cleanly without entangling a swimmer's feet?
What happens when you re-stuff a rescue throw bag by coiling the rope around your elbow instead of feeding it strand by strand?

extra_misconceptions.fact: An upstream V warns of a rock or obstruction just below the surface, while a downstream V points into the open channel.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An upstream-pointing V on the water surface marks the deepest, safest chute through a boulder garden.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Current pushes hardest against the outside bend, often sweeping boats into undercut banks or strainers along the shore.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The fastest and safest line around a sharp river bend always runs along the outside bank where the channel is widest.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A flat horizon line indicates a sudden vertical drop, ledge, or low-head dam that requires immediate scouting from shore.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A smooth, uniform horizon line across the entire river means the water ahead is flat and calm.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Eddies contain calm, upstream-flowing water behind obstacles and provide safe stopping points for scouting or resting.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Eddies behind midstream boulders pull boats downward and must be avoided during a Class II descent.

extra_socratic_questions: Which surface V-shape indicates a clean, deep channel between two submerged boulders rather than an obstacle?
Where along a Class II rapid should you catch an eddy to maintain line-of-sight with the next clear drop?
What river gauge reading in cubic feet per second turns a friendly Class II wave train into a retentive hole?
Why is it dangerous to paddle near a partially submerged tree on the outside bend of a fast-moving channel?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A 90-degree angle exposes the full side of the hull to the current and sweeps the boat downstream instead of across.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Paddling directly perpendicular to the current is the fastest way to ferry across a swift river channel.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tilting into the turn lifts the upstream edge so the opposing current passes beneath the hull without flipping the craft.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaning away from the direction of an eddy turn keeps the canoe or kayak stable as it crosses the eddy line.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wet cotton absorbs water and strips body heat rapidly, whereas synthetic fleece, neoprene, or drywear retains insulation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cotton hoodies and jeans provide reliable warmth on cool spring rivers as long as you wear a splash jacket.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Properly inflated flotation bags displace water so the swamped hull rides high and remains light enough to maneuver to shore.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Air bags inside a whitewater canoe only serve to keep the boat from sinking to the river bottom after a capsize.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your hull if you lean upstream instead of downstream while carving a sharp eddy turn?
Under what condition does an upstream ferry require a wider angle to the current than a tight eddy peel-out?
What combined air and water temperature threshold requires paddlers to wear a wetsuit or drysuit on moving water?
Which physical check confirms your Type III PFD and hull flotation bags will stay secure during a turbulent swim?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standing in moving water risks fatal foot entrapment between rocks; swimmers must float on their backs with feet downstream.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimmers in rapids should immediately stand up to walk out before the current carries them farther downstream.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Floating face-first forces water over your head as the rope tensions; roll onto your back and hold the line at your chest.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Grabbing a rescue rope while floating on your stomach lets you kick harder toward the rescuer on shore.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Securing a tensioned river line to your body prevents quick release and can drag the rescuer into the rapid.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tying the bitter end of a throw bag around your waist prevents losing the rope when catching a heavy swimmer.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Remaining upstream of a swamped hull prevents being crushed if the heavy boat pins against a midstream boulder.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Staying downstream of your swamped canoe during a capsize shields your body from approaching rocks.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to stand up in moving water that is deeper than your knees after a wet exit?
Over which shoulder should a swimmer hold a rescue rope while being pendulum-swung toward the left riverbank?
What distance and timing cues tell a shore rescuer when to shout and launch a throw bag to a swimmer in current?
What happens to a shore rescuer who wraps a throw rope around their wrist or clips it to a fixed carabiner?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Whitewater trip schedules must account for current speed, scouting stops, eddy hopping, and potential portage delays.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Calculating river trip duration uses the same average miles-per-hour pace as flatwater lake canoeing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A complete float plan documents intermediate road crossings, evacuation trails, and local hospital routes along the canyon.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Listing only the put-in and final takeout coordinates on the float plan is sufficient for emergency responders.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An experienced sweep boat must always paddle last to assist swimmers and keep stragglers between the lead and sweep craft.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Putting the least experienced paddlers in the last boat allows everyone else to watch them from downstream.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Roaring whitewater drowns out human voices, requiring standardized Pealess whistle blasts and high-visibility paddle signals.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Voice commands carry clearly over Class II rapids as long as boats remain within fifty yards of each other.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should the lead boat and sweep boat position themselves when guiding a patrol through a blind Class II rapid?
Why does a six-hour whitewater trip plan require logging intermediate bridge access points alongside the main takeout?
What measurement confirms that recent upstream rainfall has not pushed your planned Class II section into Class III flood stage?
Which whistle blast sequence and paddle signal tells the trailing boats in your group to stop and eddy out immediately?
